sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: select and context are the two primitives that turn raw goroutine code into production-safe concurrent code. Without select you cannot multiplex channels or implement non-blocking operations. Without context you cannot propagate deadlines, cancellation, or request-scoped values across API boundaries — which means your goroutines cannot be shut down cleanly and your services fail under load. Every Go backend interview that goes beyond basics will probe how you thread context through call chains and why it matters.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Think of `select` as a channel-aware switch statement: it blocks until one of its cases is ready, then executes that case. If multiple cases are ready simultaneously, one is chosen at random — this is by design to avoid starvation. A `default` case makes select non-blocking (poll, don't wait). `context.Context` is an immutable, tree-structured cancellation signal: `WithCancel` creates a child that can be cancelled manually; `WithTimeout` and `WithDeadline` set time-based cancellation; `WithValue` attaches request-scoped data. Cancellation propagates down the tree — cancelling a parent cancels all descendants.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **select statement**: blocks on multiple channel operations simultaneously; exits on the first ready case.
- **default case**: makes select non-blocking — executes immediately if no channel is ready; use for polling patterns.
- **context.WithCancel**: returns a child ctx and a `cancel()` function; always `defer cancel()` to release resources.
- **context.WithTimeout / WithDeadline**: automatically cancel after a duration or absolute time; underlying timer is cleaned up when cancel is called.
- **context.WithValue**: attaches key-value pairs; keys must be unexported types (not strings) to avoid collisions across packages.
- **Propagating context**: pass `ctx` as the first parameter of every function in the call chain — store it in a struct only when implementing an interface that requires it.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Calling cancel() twice is safe**: `cancel` is idempotent — calling it multiple times is harmless and the context is already done after the first call.
- **context.WithValue key collision**: using a bare string as a key means any package can accidentally read or overwrite it; the pattern is `type contextKey struct{}` and using a private variable of that type.
- **Context in struct**: storing context in a struct is an anti-pattern per Go docs — it makes the lifetime implicit and prevents proper cancellation propagation through the call chain.
- **ctx.Done() channel**: `select { case <-ctx.Done(): return ctx.Err() }` is the canonical goroutine exit pattern.
- **context.Background() vs context.TODO()**: Background is the root for production; TODO signals "I know I need a context here but haven't wired it up yet".

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "In Go I thread context through every function call starting from the entry point — an HTTP handler gets a context from the request, and I pass it down to database calls, external API calls, and any goroutines I spawn. When the client disconnects or a deadline fires, the context is cancelled and every layer that's listening on ctx.Done() can clean up and return. I use select when I need to wait on multiple channels at once — for example, waiting for either a result channel or the context's done channel so my goroutine never leaks. One thing I'm careful about is always deferring the cancel function returned by WithCancel or WithTimeout, even if the context is cancelled elsewhere, to avoid leaking the underlying timer."
